title: Junoon
writers: Shyam Benegal; Satyadev Dubey; Ismat Chugtai; Ruskin Bond
source_material: Based on Ruskin Bond's 1978 novella A Flight of Pigeons.
lyricist: Amir Khusro; Jigar Moradabadi; Sant Kabir
character_social_background: Muslim Pathan landholding family during the 1857 rebellion
role_gist: Javed Khan is a reckless Pathan chieftain whose life revolves around his carrier pigeons until the 1857 rebellion delivers into his house an Anglo-Indian family fleeing a massacre. He seizes Ruth Labadoor and her mother from the Hindu household sheltering them, falls in love with Ruth, and is held to a bargain by her mother: the daughter's hand only if the British are defeated. His wife Firdaus watches it all.
principal_motivation: To possess Ruth, an obsession the title names.
principal_conflict: A promise contingent on a rebellion that is being lost, and a household, a wife and a brother-in-law all set against the attachment.
character_arc: From an indolent aristocrat indifferent to politics to a man whose private obsession is destroyed with the rebellion he half-joined for it.
moral_alignment: Coercive, within a sympathetic and tragic frame
character_outcome: His pigeons freed by his brother-in-law as the Indian defeat becomes certain, and the bargain with it.
critical_reception: Widely admired. In a retrospective review Raja Sen of Rediff.com called it an overwhelmingly powerful film and a bittersweet, entirely futile love story. The Hindu's Blast from the Past notice calls Nafisa Ali's Ruth Labadoor brilliantly played and perfect in her role as a bewildered and panic-stricken girl, finds Kapoor and Jennifer Kendal giving a stellar display of their acting skills, and records convincing performances from Naseeruddin Shah, Kulbhushan Kharbanda, Ismat Chughtai and Tom Alter.
recognition: Won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Hindi, presented to Kapoor as producer, along with Best Cinematography for Govind Nihalani and Best Audiography. At the 27th Filmfare Awards it won Best Film for Kapoor, Best Director for Shyam Benegal, Best Dialogue, Best Cinematography, Best Editing and Best Sound Recording, with nominations for Naseeruddin Shah, Jennifer Kendal and Ruskin Bond. It was the inaugural film of the 7th International Film Festival of India in 1979, the official Indian entry at the Moscow International Film Festival, and was shown at Montreal, Cairo, Sydney and Melbourne.
research_notes: The first film Kapoor produced under Film-Valas, and the beginning of the parallel-cinema slate that runs through Kalyug, 36 Chowringhee Lane, Vijeta and Utsav. Three of his children, Sanjana, Kunal and Karan Kapoor, appear, and his wife Jennifer Kendal plays Ruth's mother, opposite whom he negotiates the film's central bargain. The Hindu's notice gives the film's box-office status as average, entered here as the verdict; phase 2 had left it undocumented, and the film's standing rests on its National Film Award rather than its collections. The notice's praise of 'Shashi Kapoor and Jennifer' refers to Jennifer Kendal as Mariam Labadoor, Ruth's mother, not to either of his romantic partners, so it is not used to assess the pairings.
